definitions.definition: The adherents' own name for Madhva's system: the doctrine that what is known through valid means is real (tattva = not superimposed), above all the reality of difference.

The usual outside name for Madhva's Vedānta, stressing real difference; Madhva himself reads 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya as what is 'known otherwise' (wrongly) and 'advaita' as the Lord who has no equal.
Whatever is real, i.e. not superimposed (anāropita) and an object of valid knowledge; twofold, independent (Viṣṇu) and dependent (everything else).
Real difference, which is the very nature (svarūpa) of each thing, grasped together with the thing itself; not a separate negation (anyonyābhāva). Fivefold and eternal between God, souls and matter.
The five real and eternal differences: soul–Lord, soul–soul, matter–Lord, matter–matter and matter–soul; they hold in all states, including liberation.
That which depends on nothing else for its being, knowledge and activity: Viṣṇu alone.
All reality other than Viṣṇu — Lakṣmī, souls, matter, time, the Veda, negations — which exists, knows and acts only as dependent on and controlled by him.

A dependent reality of three kinds: prior non-existence, destruction and constant (absolute) non-existence; mutual non-existence (difference) is not a fourth, being the nature of things. Known by inference and by perception.
Sentient dependent beings: Lakṣmī (eternally untouched by sorrow) and all souls, divided by their relation to sorrow and their fitness.
Insentient reality: eternal (the Vedas), eternal-and-non-eternal (Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti), and non-eternal products, uncompounded and compounded.
The beginningless, unalterable gradation of souls in nature, knowledge, bliss and office, from the lowest to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; it continues in liberation.
The gradation of the bliss enjoyed by the liberated, each class a hundredfold above the one below.
Souls whose intrinsic nature fits them for liberation: gods, sages, ancestors, rulers and the best humans (the 'sāttvika' souls).

equivalents.note: Jain 'bhavya' (capable of liberation) is analogous to 'mukti-yogya'; Dvaita grounds it in intrinsic nature and grace.

definitions.definition: Souls unfit both for liberation and for blinding darkness, who remain forever in transmigration (the middling humans); Tattvasaṅkhyāna calls them 'sṛti-saṃsthita', Tattvaviveka 'nityāvarta'.

equivalents.note: Jain 'abhavya' souls, never able to attain liberation, are analogous to Dvaita's souls unfit for liberation; the grounds (karma-theory vs innate fitness) differ.

definitions.definition: Souls whose nature destines them for eternal blinding darkness: daityas, rākṣasas, piśācas and the lowest humans.
The eternal state of sorrow without return reached by the souls fit for darkness, especially through hatred of Hari and his devotees.
A soul's innate, beginningless capacity, which fixes its destiny and the office, worship and vision it may attain; to desire what one is unfit for leads to a fall.
A separate class of gods fit for the office of Brahmā (Vāyu is among them); only they can reach that office.
Lakṣmī (Śrī, Ramā), the one dependent sentient being who is eternally untouched by sorrow and never bound.
Viṣṇu's consort, eternally free and dependent, the 'akṣara' whose body never perishes, higher than all souls in every quality; as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā she is the higher prakṛti (śakti).
All souls whose bodies perish — Brahmā, Śiva, the gods and the rest.
Lakṣmī, whose body is imperishable; beyond her is Hari (Puruṣottama).
Viṣṇu, beyond both the perishable (souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī).
The one independent reality, full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of defects, the Brahman of the Upaniṣads and the primary meaning of all words.

literal: resting-place of beings / of the waters

definitions.definition: Name of Viṣṇu most used by Madhva in his invocations: full of qualities, free of defects, known only through the true scriptures.
Name of Viṣṇu in the formula 'Hari is supreme over all' (Hari-sarvottama); controller of all, under whom all dependent reality stands.
The central tenet that Viṣṇu is supreme over all beings; the 'great purport' (mahātātparya) of all scripture.
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), highest of souls, equal in rank with Brahmā, surpassed only by Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu; paired in the formula 'Hari-sarvottama, Vāyu-jīvottama'.
The deity Vāyu, highest soul, giver of liberation by Viṣṇu's permission, whose three avatāras are Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva.
Vāyu as the chief vital breath presiding in all bodies; name under which he is worshipped (Hanumān shrines of the tradition).

equivalents.standpoint: Dvaita reads the Upaniṣadic chief breath as the deity Vāyu
equivalents.note: The Upaniṣadic 'mukhya prāṇa' is, for Dvaita, the highest soul Vāyu presiding over breath.

definitions.definition: In Dvaita the word applies primarily to Viṣṇu alone, 'full' (pūrṇa) in qualities; defined as that from which come creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release.
Viṣṇu's possession of infinite auspicious qualities, each unlimited; the reason he is called 'great' (Brahman).
Viṣṇu's freedom from every defect, even in his avatāras, whose apparent sufferings are shown to delude the unfit.
Read by Dvaita as 'free of the qualities of prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas)'; the Advaita reading 'without any attributes' is rejected as against scripture and reason.
Difference within Viṣṇu (between him and his qualities, acts, forms or avatāras), declared unreal; apparent distinctions are explained by viśeṣa.

In Madhva's usage a 'substitute for difference' (bheda-pratinidhi): the capacity that allows a thing to be spoken of as distinct from its lasting properties (or God from his qualities and forms) where there is no real difference.
Viṣṇu's manifestation of his own eternal body of consciousness and bliss, not a birth of flesh; the avatāras are wholly identical with him and flawless.
Viṣṇu's special presence in a soul (as distinct from an avatāra); one must know which beings are his avatāras and which are only his āveśas.
Viṣṇu's agency in the creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release of the world (Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light).
An eternal, sentient, dependent self, atomic, distinct from God and from every other soul, a reflection (pratibimba) of God, with an innate fitness that fixes its destiny.
God as the original of which the soul is the reflection; the Lord in one's heart contemplated as 'you are the bimba, I am the reflection'.

The soul as reflection of God — dependent on its original, similar to it and eternally different from it; the 'adjunct' that makes it a reflection is its own nature, so the reflection is eternal (not produced by an external upādhi as in Advaita).
The Advaita notion that the soul is Brahman limited by adjuncts, refuted in the Upādhikhaṇḍana: ignorance cannot belong to the all-knower, and adjuncts cannot account for it.

The soul's own intrinsic faculty of awareness (its 'essential sense'), counted as the seventh kind of perception; it apprehends the self, the mind and its states, time, space and the validity of knowledge, and what it establishes is never sublated.
What accords with its object (yathārtha); twofold — valid knowledge itself (kevala) and its means (anupramāṇa).
Knowledge that accords with its object, of four grades: the Lord's, Lakṣmī's, the yogins' and others'.
The means that produce valid knowledge: perception, inference and authoritative word (presumption and comparison fall under inference).
The faultless contact of sense and object; sevenfold — the witness (sākṣin) and six senses (five outer and manas).
Faultless reasoning (upapatti) based on invariable concomitance; includes presumption and comparison.
Faultless speech; above all the authorless Veda and the other true scriptures, the only means by which Viṣṇu is known.
Validity of knowledge belongs to it by itself (and is apprehended by the witness); invalidity comes from extraneous defects.
The Veda's character of having no author, not even God; its words and order are eternal.
The Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the entire Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas of that character and whatever follows them.
Texts other than and contrary to the true scriptures; Janārdana is not known through them; some are said to have been produced to delude.
The intended import of a text, known by the marks (opening and close, repetition, novelty, result, praise, reasoning); the 'great purport' of all scripture is Viṣṇu's supremacy.
The doctrine that every word, and every letter, primarily designates Viṣṇu, and only secondarily other things.

The designator of Viṣṇu, eightfold (a, u, m and five further subtle components up to 'atiśānta'), naming his forms Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman and Jñānātman; source of the other mantras.
The form of Viṣṇu that presides over the soul's waking state.
The form of Viṣṇu that, abiding in the mind, creates the soul's dreams.
The form of Viṣṇu that presides over deep sleep, in which the soul, covered by tamas, rests in him.
The form of Viṣṇu at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated and occasionally seen by the fully concentrated with direct vision; it gives the liberated their knowledge and activity.
The eternal material cause of the world, insentient and dependent, presided over by Lakṣmī (as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā); God is the efficient cause only.
An eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep.
A real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold: one covering the soul's own nature and qualities, one covering (the soul's knowledge of) the Supreme; removed only by the Lord.
In Madhva's usage chiefly God's will (icchā) or wisdom, and also prakṛti; not an indeterminable illusion. The 'māyā' of the Advaitins is identified polemically with the Buddhist saṃvṛti.
Dvaita's name for Advaita Vedānta (its adherents 'māyins'), whose tenets — the world's falsity, the indeterminable, identity of soul and Brahman — are refuted.
The Advaita claim that the world is false; Dvaita refutes the proposed definitions and the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness.
The Advaita category of what is neither real nor unreal; for Dvaita it is established by no means of knowledge and taught by no scripture.
The Advaita doctrine that the world is an apparent transformation of Brahman; rejected because the witness establishes the world's reality.
Wrong knowledge — for Madhva the real sense of 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya: the soul's misapprehension (of its relation to the body and to God), which ceases by God's will when he is known.
Impressions of past experience; the material from which dreams are really produced (dreams are therefore not false).
The internal sense (the sixth, after the five outer senses), a non-eternal product of prakṛti (with mahat, ahaṃkāra and buddhi); memory arises from mental perception.
The hundred and one channels of the heart, one (suṣumnā) going to the crown, by which the knower departs at death with the help of Hari in the heart; the suṣumnā 'shines' in the seated worshipper.

Firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation, to which all other practices are subsidiary, and itself eternal bliss in liberation.
Understanding of Viṣṇu's supremacy and perfection, which must precede and ground bhakti.
The love that, grounded in knowledge of God's greatness, firm and greater than all other love, constitutes bhakti.

Viṣṇu's grace, without which there is no liberation; lowest when won by ritual (giving heaven), middling by hearing etc., highest by fullness of knowledge (giving liberation); it reaches lower beings through the higher.

equivalents.note: Both name divine grace; in Dvaita prasāda is won by knowledge and devotion and graded, so the overlap is partial.

definitions.definition: Knowledge of Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences and gradation, culminating in direct knowledge (aparokṣa); it wins the abundant grace that alone liberates.
Direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of God — in the form of one's own original (bimba), to the extent one's fitness allows — produced by meditation built on hearing and reflection.

equivalents.note: Dvaita uses aparokṣa-jñāna and sākṣātkāra (direct realization) of God interchangeably.

definitions.definition: Study of the true scriptures and their correct interpretation from a teacher; the first principal means to knowledge, never to be reduced.
Reasoned reflection on what was heard, removing doubts (e.g. with companions); a principal means to knowledge.
Sustained meditation on Viṣṇu with his qualities, according to one's fitness, which produces direct knowledge; not a mere subsidiary of hearing.
Worship of Hari with the qualities appropriate to one's fitness — Brahmā with all qualities, humans as bliss, knower and the ever-existing Self.

Eligibility for knowledge and scripture, in three grades (low, middle, highest) by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant devoted to Viṣṇu. Eligibility to Veda, Tantra or the Name is distinguished by class and gender.
Acting without desire for results, offering all acts to Hari as their real doer; with flawless service and fitness, a condition of seeing Hari.

Action and its residue; it cannot be exhausted by experience because new karma is always made, so liberation comes by grace through knowledge, while ritual action at best wins the lowest grace (heaven).

The soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss in the Lord's presence, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing; forms: sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya.
The bliss intrinsic to each soul, enjoyed unobstructed in liberation in the measure of its fitness.
Form of liberation: dwelling in the Lord's world.
Form of liberation: dwelling near the Lord.
Form of liberation: bearing a form like the Lord's.
Form of liberation in which the liberated enter the Lord's body and come out again, enjoying with him — without identity.
The knower's departure from the body through the crown channel, when the tip of the heart lights up, aided by the grace of Hari in the heart.

literal: the path of light (beginning with flame)

definitions.definition: The path by which the knowers go to Brahmā's world, from which they reach the Supreme with Brahmā at the great dissolution.
Debate aimed only at ascertaining the truth, as between teacher and disciple.
Debate aimed at victory, one of the three kinds of debate among the learned.
Debate that only attacks the opponent's position, one of the three kinds of debate.
Initiation into Hari's worship and mantra by the ācārya (with the sipping of the Lord's foot-water and vows); those without it are called 'beasts among men'.

The teacher from whose grace the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge; the lineage runs from Nārāyaṇa and Vyāsa through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; devotion to the teacher as to God is enjoined.
The eleventh lunar day of both fortnights, kept by fasting, with detailed rules for days overlapped by the tenth.
Kṛṣṇa's birthday when the dark eighth coincides with Rohiṇī at midnight; kept by fasting.
The upright forehead mark of the Vaiṣṇava, made with gopīcandana clay; praised as purifying and required for rites to bear fruit.
The rotation of the worship of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi among the eight maṭhas; now two years per maṭha (a change credited to Vādirāja Tīrtha).
The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi founded by Madhva's eight ascetic disciples.
In Mādhva usage the tomb-shrine of an ascetic saint, where the tradition holds the saint to remain present (e.g. Rāghavendra at Mantrālaya, Vyāsatīrtha at Nava Brindāvana).
The collection of Madhva's thirty-seven works.
Direct realization of the Lord produced by meditation built on hearing and reflection; used interchangeably with aparokṣa-jñāna.
